utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I brought the cross-examination to a conclusion at 20 to 2.00 on the last sitting day of last week partly because it seemed a convenient time to end and realised on reflection that with your leave there are a few more questions I should ask for two distinct reasons. One, there are simply a couple of points that I ought to have put that I didn't; but two, when it comes to the discussion of the potential exhibits, our case is contained in documents, possible witness statements and schedules that may not be admitted as exhibits or otherwise documentary material in the case, and unless I put my case on the record in question form, then it won't be on the record at all. So with your leave, I would ask a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. As to the translation of the medical documents, they are, I hope, on their way pretty well immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I will try to deal with this as succinctly as possible through the schedule. May the witness have the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, I realised over the weekend there were a few more questions I should have asked of you and the Court has given me leave to ask them. Would you look, please, at the schedule and you understand and remember the way the schedule is constructed. If we look on the first page, we see crosses in the fourth line of Sali Emini. Sali Emini is dead; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sali Emini was, you say, an informant, but you produce no evidence of his being a registered informant, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as an informant is concerned, probably you could request that through official channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You produce --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, rather, by our secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you remember that I asked you to produce your diaries and you didn't do so. There's no evidence of what he was paid, if anything, for being an informant?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last time I don't know whether he was paid, but quite certainly our secretariat will provide you confirmation saying that he was an informant, and you can request that through official channels because, as I say, I wasn't able to bring that logbook or register with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's the alleged source of no less than 11 of your reports. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but in my Official Notes he provided information in notes where his name is mentioned as well as in some other notebooks where it states that an interview was conducted with a person from the village of Racak, Stimlje municipality. I can't tell you exactly which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The court record, 2.5, 2.6, 2.7, 2.8, 2.10, 2.13, 2.15, 2.18, 2.19, 2.22, 2.30. And significantly this, Mr. Jasovic: When you were first asked about 2.23, who we looked at last week in some detail, you initially gave a different name as the provider or different identity as the provider of this statement. You then provided the name of Emini and you then suggested that there were two sources for 2.23, although the document doesn't say as much. Can you explain why you gave different accounts of Emini's contribution to 2.23?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, because I have a large number of Official Notes at my disposal, information, and statements, however, on the first day I said -- well, I can't remember. I think the first day I said -- I was speaking about the male nurse, and the second day I said and -- or, rather, when I looked at this piece of information at my hotel, tab 2.23, the same knowledge was provided by two sources, the same information, which means the male nurse and the informant. They provided the same information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The piece of paper 2.23 doesn't remotely make it clear that it's two sources of information that you're relying on, does it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have the right to that in my Official Note or piece of information. I cannot mention a name at all, and I need not say. I don't have to say which sources provided me with the information, with the intelligence, because I didn't write down those Official Notes or notes for the purposes of this trial at all. So I have the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, we have some information, which is dealt with in the witness statement of one of the investigators, some confidential information to the effect that far from being an informant he may have not been a collaborator at all. This can be found in the investigator's note of Howard Tucker.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know which note you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, let's -- let's just look at page 1 of the schedule very briefly. If you've got that in front of you. You see Emini's name appears for two people here, but it's right, isn't it, that there is no signed document for Emini so far as informations dealing with Racak victims is concerned. There's no signature of Emini anywhere on those documents.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, pursuant to our instructions and pursuant to the law on criminal proceedings, it doesn't say that persons that you conduct an interview with and compile an Official Note on should sign the document. Nowhere does it say that except a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look down to Zeqiri Sabit, the Court may wish to register that this one is signed although the statement-maker says that he was badly beaten, and it only deals with, because we've been as inclusive as possible in identifying possible connections to the KLA, and this identifies Ajet Emini as loaning a car to the KLA. That's the height of what's said here. So in this statement where it's said that Ajet Emini loaned a car to the KLA, he accepts that he signed it but he was badly beaten by you. What do you say to that concerning Sabit Zeqiri?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not true that he was beaten, and I stand by -- well, I haven't got the statement in front of me. I'd like to have a look at it. But I stand by the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 of the schedule. The only reference on page 2 as the Court will see is right at the top, Taib Maljici. I think the date is wrong. It's not the 1st of September I think it's the 18th of September but it's still in the correct place in the sequence. This is a statement by Maljici Taib, somebody we've been unable to locate at all. You say that in his statement he identified Mehmeti Bajram as the person who you saw in Laniste. Your Honours, this is a case where we say there may be a mistake in identity. The high point of your evidence about somebody called Bajram Mehmeti is you saw him in Laniste; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in Laniste so how could I personally see Bajram Mehmeti in Laniste.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we go to page 3 of the schedule. The third and fourth rows relate to Sali Emini and none of those informations is signed. Likewise, the one about six or seven lines further on for the -- for 2.22, the 29th of December of 1998, that also is unsigned; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said a moment ago that the person you interview doesn't -- that the person doesn't sign the Official Note or piece of information. I think that I was clear there. Regardless of whether it is an informant, a friendly contact or any other form of contact. So in the Official Note or piece of information on the basis of the interview the person conducting the interview doesn't sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one, --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who gives the interview doesn't sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Faik Ramadani, has denied that the signature is his, says he was beaten by you and saw blood on the floor. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. But Mr. Prosecutor, you're giving me some names and I haven't got the document in front of me. How can I answer your questions if I can't see those names? I don't know whether I actually conducted interviews with the persons you're mentioning now or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course you don't have any recollection of them, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember. I can't remember every individual. Probably I will remember some of them, but as I said, there were over 700 statements taken, whereas you're now asking me these questions, and I can't just tell you off the top of my head. I don't have the notes. I don't have the names, so how can I tell you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you be in a better position to respond to the Prosecutor's questions if you had the documents in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, of course I would have to look at the document first, whether I took a statement from the individual or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll hand that to him, Your Honours. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness have the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we dealt with this signature during your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We did, yes but [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1.35, which we've recorded as referring to both Ragip Bajrami and Bajram Mehmeti -- in fact, the high point of your material about Ragip Bajrami is that he was at a checkpoint, and the high point of your material against Bajram Mehmeti is that he provided food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Let me take a look at the document and see what it says in the document. The fact is that both were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you say. Well, just look at the detail, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which tab do you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1.35. It was open at the right page for you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At tab 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was open at the right page for you. 1.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here I have Faik Ramadani as the person. Faik Ramadani. Is that what you're asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you look down on about the fourth paragraph you'll see that you claim that Faik Ramadani said that he saw Bajram Mehmeti at the checkpoint, in uniform with insignia and rifle. And if you go over to the second to last paragraph you'll see that you say of Ragip Bajrami that he goes to the houses of inhabitants and provides food.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Prosecutor. There's a terrorism here and aiding and abetting. And if he provided food -- well, he was a member of the KLA, and he was a member of the KLA --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- one person distributed food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How are you a member of the KLA by distributing food?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this person doesn't appear only in this statement. He appears in other documents as well. I don't have them at hand here so I can't remember off the top of my head but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we look at the next one -- can you move on to 1.38, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pausing there, can I get an observation from the witness. If the usher could put this document on the ELMO, please. This is a commented B/C/S version of his statement, 1.35. Mr. Jasovic, do you see the -- a signature on the left bottom of the -- of Mr. Ramadani, which is written in Cyrillic letters? You said that this is a signature of that witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This statement was shown to the -- Mr. Ramadani allegedly by Mr. Barney Kelly, an investigator of the OTP, and Mr. Ramadani signed his signature on the topside of this document, left. Could you see the top left? If the usher could show it. Yes. You see the note? You note Barney Kelly's signature and underneath you see Faik Ramadani. Do you think it is a signature of the same person? What is your observation on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can guarantee that the statement given by Ramadani Faik, and I explained this last time, that persons of -- middle-aged people, that is to say over the age of 50, usually sign their names in Cyrillic, in the Cyrillic script. Now, as far as the statement of Faik Ramadani is concerned, you can carry out an expertise. Bring in a handwriting expert and somebody can ascertain whether it is indeed his signature or not. But quite certainly it is his signature, because I know all the individuals, all the people -- or, rather, I know that everybody of middle age tends to sign their names in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just draw your attention to what you've just shown us on the overhead projector under Barney Kelly's signature. It says the name of this individual and it is written in capital letters. So quite obviously it cannot be his signature. Nobody signs their signature with -- using capital letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidently, your observation that they choose to right in Cyrillic, the language of the Serbs, is a nonsense in the same way as your suggestion that they speak Serb. They speak Kosovo Albanian, don't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not true, Mr. Prosecutor. Well, I don't remember whether he -- but as I say, generally elderly persons do know the Serbian language. Now, as far as his signature is concerned, I'm not here to decide -- I don't decide whether he chooses to sign in the Cyrillic or Latin script. He gave his signature and placed his signature voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is one other tiny point I wanted to deal with at some stage. I'll deal with it now before we return to the chart. Every one of these statements deals with the phrase "so-called KLA," a phrase you weren't able remember in Albanian last week. Can you remember it this week?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can't remember now either. I didn't give it that much thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know astatukja [phoen]. Astatukja, something like that, in that kind of term -- in those kind of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of course they didn't. That little phrase alone shows that all these statements are simply concoctions of yours, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not through, Mr. Prosecutor, because -- or, rather, they emphasised that it was their so-called -- that's what they called it. So they said that was their so-called, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1.38, please - will you go to that - which is the statement of Ramiz Roshaj. This man says he was threatened but not beaten, and it doesn't say that you were present, but if we just look at the statement to see what we've got here by way of completeness, under Muhamet Ismajlji's name the maximum that is said about Muhamet Ismajlji, this is on the second page of the English, towards the end of the B/C/S, is that he was a member, and can you see that? It's just a list of people. One of whom is Muhamet Ismajlji, said to be a member of the KLA in Malopoljce.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Musliu Muhamed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as the other names listed, Your Honours, that is Jashar Salihu. Just to show the maximum possible completeness. If Your Honour looks at the earlier page, you'll see a Salihaj whose first name isn't known, and that's the only reason that's been included there. So it's not -- it doesn't amount to anything like a clear identification, and I don't need to ask the witness anything about it. Can we go to the next one but two. 1.40, Bahri Hisenaj. And Your Honours, there is an error in the chart on this page. There are two crosses, and if you would delete the red cross, the left-hand side of the two crosses and move it to the right so that they are one place to the left. These two crosses should be under the names of the Metushis, Arif and Haki, and they're included there again for completeness simply on the basis that there's a reference to something happening outside the house of the brothers Metushi. That's all. So it's not any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This man, as I say, Mr. Jasovic, says that he was beaten, and the most he says --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person certainly wasn't beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he says -- apparently in his statement he says that they -- that the KLA members have a security force stationed in a house, a store owned by the Metushis. That's the limit of what is said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't follow. I don't see any crosses in Hyseni Bajram.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first item on page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're on page 3, and it's -- and it's 1.40, just before the horizontal black line or three entries before the horizontal black line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then it's the left-hand cross that should be deleted and placed to the right. That would then make an entry for the two brothers Metushi. The statement shows no more than the allegation of the use of a store of the Metushi brothers, and that's the only reason we've put them in there for completeness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what's the point you're making about the statement shows no more than. You've done this with one or more of the statements. What is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point is this: That when we you look at the last one before Racak, which you'll see is Sherif Sadiki who is himself deceased, so we haven't been able to inquire into that potential statement-maker, but all he says is that there was a brother outside the house of Sherif Sadiki, i.e., a KLA brother. So then if one reviews all the pre-Racak material, three points emerge. That's the reason I'm dealing with it. And can we then just with that look at -- well, now I'll just deal with it in this way:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sherif Sadiki, do you understand him now to be dead?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because if I take a look at my documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Our information is he is now dead. Do you challenge that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say either yes or no because I don't know. I can't remember this name and surname, Sherif Sadiki. So how can I claim anything? What I can tell you about the statement of Bahri Hisenaj, it is stated clearly here. I can tell you that in front of a bridge in the village the KLA members have their security checkpoint from which they opened fire at the members of the police. They were also located in a shop owned by Metushi from the village of Racak. As for this other person, I really can't tell you off the top of my head whether this person is alive or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, you told us last week about the number of people identified before Racak occurred, and if we look at this chart where we have included every conceivable connection to the KLA that we can, what it comes to is this: That if we put Sali Emini's unsigned material on one side, we have somebody who lent a car, an uncertain identification of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. someone called Bajram Mehmeti. We have the provision of food, and we have one allegation of Ragip Bajrami being at a checkpoint. We have an allegation of somebody, Muhamet Ismajlji being a member, we have a suggestion that two brothers' house may have been used by the KLA, and we have the evidence of one brother being outside -- one KLA brother outside the house of Lufti Bilalli, and that is all we have. Do you follow that, Mr. Jasovic? You are in --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to follow all that. What I can tell you is that the informer provided authentic and true information which can be confirmed by tab 2.30, because the informer told me that the house of Qerim Imedi [phoen] would be attacked because he had three sons serving in the MUP of Serbia. And that exactly materialised three weeks later. You're now putting a lot of questions to me, so I definitely cannot follow all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the other thing that then follows from our chart is this: That Sali Emini who you say provided this material before Racak suddenly doesn't feature again. He doesn't turn up in relation to the Racak victims at all after the Racak event itself. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, he appears before the event and after the event, I can't remember the exact date and up to which month, but I know that I spoke to him on the phone the last time in late May of 1999. I couldn't tell you now off the top of my head. If I were to look at the documents, I probably would be able to tell you. I don't know the exact date when I spoke to him last.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the next thing I wanted you just to confirm is this: We looked last week at number 1.45, which contains some alleged detail of what happened at Racak. You remember that was people found in the KLA yard, and I explained to you that they were found elsewhere. If you turn to 1.54, which is Avni Metushi and you look to his statement which is at the end of tab 1.54. And if the Court goes to the third page in English, and if you, Mr. Jasovic, go to the second page, halfway down. This witness is alleged in the statement to have said that on the 15th of January he came out of a house during the fighting in the street and he saw Sadik Mujota in uniform with a sniper rifle and his son. All right? But apart from that detail and from what we looked at in 1.45, none of your statements from these alleged volunteers says a word about the events of Racak on the 15th. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, based on this, one can see that the statement was not extorted from the statement giver. One can see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- everything was stated voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very simple question. Very simple question. You are investigating --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please tell me the passage. I wasn't able to find the passage with that text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your statement, it's on the second page, it's halfway down, and it begins "Dana, 15 January 1999," and it just deals with seeing Sadik Mujota. But my question is -- you found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And apart from what we looked at in 1.45 and despite the fact that you were seeing people on the 16th, 17th, 20th, 23rd of January, and so on, no one gives any detail of what allegedly happened in Racak. You were investigating the event. Can you explain why not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the question? You mean about the 15th of January, how that transpired on the spot? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. How did you, an investigator, seeing people from Racak, seeing people who had been involved and suffering and left dead and so on, can you explain how you only got these two statements that say anything about what happened at Racak? One of them we looked at, 1.45, and said is -- we suggest to you is completely wrong and made up, and the other one, 1.54, has one sentence. Can you explain how the investigating --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. It's not true that this was invented. I don't know if this involves two statements or more statements. I simply can't remember. But this statement is authentic as far as I am concerned and true, what this person stated. My colleagues and I who took this statement stand by it because this is what was indeed stated. I can't now tell you why he did not explain how the event actually unfolded. I don't know. I don't know. I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if you look at the chart, we've already looked at it mostly, but if you look at it, please, I'm going to run through it very quickly. My suggestion to you is that claiming to have got identification of all these Racak victims as early as the 16th from Mustafa Afrim who it is suggested was beaten, Rama Shaban on the 16th who I suggest to you was beaten, and Muhadin Xheladini on the 17th who was forced to sign by seeing blood on the floor, I suggest that those three as an example are just examples of statements that you've --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Prosecutor. That's not true. This is simply your opinion, but it's not true. It's not true. Why don't you prove it to me that he was beaten and beaten up? Why didn't he report that? If he was indeed beaten, why didn't he report that to my superiors, and later on, after our departure, why didn't he report that to the KFOR and UNMIK and other competent authorities? I can tell you now that you extorted a statement from him, but that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that it was taken under any duress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please. Make good your assertion that I, or it may be we, I don't know what you mean, extorted a statement from him. Just explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am explaining that the statement was taken accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure in prescribed form. And I can confirm the authenticity of that statement. I don't know how else to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've chosen to make an allegation against either me or the investigators of the Prosecution. You said that a statement has been extorted. Please make good your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming, Mr. Prosecutor, that you extorted these statements from the witnesses, but, I understand these people. I understand why they had to deny their own statements. That's quite natural, because otherwise they would have had problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would face adverse consequences, they and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Jasovic, don't you, that there's no allegation that I've put to you that isn't based on material that has been provided to me from our investigators or other sources, none. Now, you were able to make an allegation against me with absolutely no material to back it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure if that's exactly how he intended what he said to be interpreted. He says: "I can tell you now that you extorted a statement from him, but that's not true." In other words, he may be saying that's a mere allegation. "It's easy for me to say it."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll move on. I can't pursue --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that's the view the Court wants to take of this, I shan't take any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at page 4 of this schedule. You see -- if you look at --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me make it quite plain to you, Mr. Jasovic, I don't accept that interpretation, and I think you were only too willing to make an allegation without any foundation but I'm going to move on from there. If we look at page 4 of this schedule and if we cast our eyes down, 2.23 and then 1.5 --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not prepared, Mr. Prosecutor. What I'm prepared to say or, rather, to inquire how come these people did not report these cases after our departure to competent authorities and so on? Why wasn't this reported to our superiors? Because the statement with Afrim Mustafa was taken on the 16th of January, 1999. So they could have reported that to our superiors or perhaps to UNMIK, to KFOR, to other institutions after our departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As for dealing with your superiors or any part of the police force, shall we just look back and see what had been the practice of the organs of the police and indeed of the judiciary for those who even managed to get complaints on? Can we go just very briefly back to volume 2 of your materials if the Court has it, at tab 21. I'll read it out to you. It's part of a human rights report. It happens to concern a policeman called Jasovic, probably not you, in fact it doesn't appear to be you, because it comes from somewhere else. And this was as long ago as 1993. It can be found at page 19. And on this occasion -- do you remember this incident? This was two police officers and it was in Prizren. The pathologist was Dobricanin and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 21?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 21 at page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. In which case we'll lay it on the overhead projector, if we've got it, exhibit 1.45, and I can lay my bit on the overhead projector. Very easy to do. I wasn't expecting to cover this, but since the witness makes the observations he does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Part of "Under Orders."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. No, it's the next -- it's the next exhibit. I'll give the exhibit number in just a second. Could you just lay that on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is from a Human Rights Watch report. It's about an officer called Jasovic and another officer called Kosovic who beat someone to death. Next page, please. They were incited. Now, next page, please, Mr. Nort. On the indictment which cited them for beating the man who died with blows on his feet and palms of his hand, what happened at the trial was that policemen greeted the accused warmly. They had a short trial. For killing someone in detention they were sentenced to three years' imprisonment and then immediately released on appeal. Who knows whether they were ever re-imprisoned. No one would be able -- with the culture of police violence that prevailed in your country at that time, no one would go and complain to superiors officers, would they? It would be inviting yet more violence. Do you remember this police trial with somebody the same name as you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, first of all what you stated previously is not true. Secondly, I've no idea what trial you're talking about. You are now putting some documents to me and I know nothing about them. I don't know what happened, what transpired. Based on what I can see, it says here the 23rd of November, 1993. I have no idea what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was provided from the book which is in English. I think it would be only proper to have this read out to Mr. Jasovic, the quotation that was just read out to him, because the only words that he can understand here, the only word is the word Jasovic. So he needs to know what Mr. Nice is claiming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea what this trial was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that as long ago as 1993 policemen such as your fellow-named policeman Jasovic who killed people in custody could reasonably expect a warm court hearing and release on appeal after a short sentence. Does that fit with your understanding of the way the police were able to operate in Kosovo in the mid-1990s?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you're asking me questions now and I don't know this policeman Jasovic. I don't know about this case. I don't know where this happened. I simply am unable to answer. You are putting some documents to me that I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the document on the ELMO says that they were sentenced to three years in prison but immediately released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Pending appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Pending appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that you put --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- said released on appeal you meant they were released pending appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pending appeal. And it's part of Exhibit 205, a Human Rights Watch report. Can I have it back, please, Mr. Nort, and I'll just rapidly deal with the rest of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because if you'll be good enough, please, Mr. Jasovic, to look at page 4 of the schedule you'll see as we can all see that following what you claim were your successful results on the 16th and 17th you then get very, very full returns from 2.23, from 1.50, from 1.51, all of whom claim that their statements are untrue. 2.23 we've dealt with. 1.50 we've dealt with. He denies the statement was his in any form. 1.51 says that he was beaten and forced to sign his statement. You needed this material and you forced these statements into existence one way or another, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Prosecutor. That's not true, not at all. I've stated here a number of times that I know why they refused to confirm the authenticity of their own statement, Official Note, or any other document. I am telling you now that no statements were extorted. There was no duress. No force was used against them let alone torture. This information, as far as I'm concerned, is true and authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, would you just state again why in your view they refused to confirm the authenticity of their statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor -- Mr. President, I know because after we left a number of Albanians were killed precisely for those reasons. I can't now recall all of the cases, but let me tell you, their families would first of all be isolated, ostracised, which would be the hardest possible thing for an Albanian family. They wouldn't be able to marry off their children. Second, their security, their safety would be endangered. And I know the customs of Albanians. They value the safety of their families very highly, and this is the reason why they cannot confirm the authenticity of their statements. To this day there are families that are involved in a blood feud, and there's a vendetta. I'm stating this with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say that you are aware that a number of Albanians were killed precisely for those reasons. What reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, let me explain this briefly. After we left, the former KLA members joined the secret police, KZK and other extreme organisations. The secret police conducts checks on the ground, and in order to obtain information about Albanians who provided information to us, who were friendly with the Serbs, who were friendly with the SUP members and Albanians who refused to join the KLA. I can tell you in this particular case my informer contacted me in late May of 1999 and told me on the phone, he said, "I'm being threatened by Albanians, Dragan." I told him to go into hiding and that it wouldn't last longer than three days. However, he was brought into Kosovo from Macedonia on a false pretext, and he was killed in front of his family home in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You also said earlier in response to a question from the Prosecutor that none of these Albanians who claim that they were beaten made any report either to your superiors or to UNMIK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, no, because most likely UNMIK would forward that to the Ministry of the Interior, and I would be interviewed regarding that. If indeed these persons, as they are claiming, went to speak to the competent authorities in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The people about whom you're making these extraordinary allegations include medically qualified people, schoolteachers. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know all of their professions. Once again, you are putting questions to me that I can't answer. I interviewed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of various professional backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've had evidence -- not evidence. There's material that I put to you in part that I must summarise a little more to the suggestion that people were electrocuted. The medical person who has been spoken to produces this as the photograph of one person who had electrodes placed on his feet. Does that resemble what you saw done to people in custody? Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Prosecutor. I don't even know who this is about. I'm not sure about the authenticity of this photograph. I'm telling you, it's not true that any of them were subjected to electrical shocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can find reference to electrocution at 1.33, 1.43, 1.54 and independently in the report from 1995 and independently from Defence witnesses -- or one Defence witness in KLA case here, the Limaj case. So that's at least five different sources for electrocution. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that it's not true that any electrical shocks were administered. I don't know what I need to tell you about 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've got baseball bat allegations coming from independently from 1.51, 1.53 and 2.23 at least independently. Can you explain how three different people spoken to on different occasions without being able to contact each other refer to baseball bats? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true that there were any baseball bats. I never held a baseball bat in my hand, and I didn't even have an official baton in my office let alone a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Jasovic, just this: There's a lot of evidence before the Court it would be for the learned Judges to decide in due course but from cartridge cases, bullets, other forensic scientific findings, there's a lot of forensic scientific material to show that the people died where they were found, that they had been ambushed or simply shot defenselessly. Your investigation didn't deal with the forensic scientific findings at all, did it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the office using information about the movements, activities, numbers, and potential perpetrators of terrorist attacks. That's what I worked with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simply concerned fraudulently, criminally, and as necessary to provide bits of paper that suggested those who died in Racak were members of the KLA and that's what you did.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true, Mr. Prosecutor, what you're putting to me. I stand by all of my documents, all Official Notes, all documents entitled information and so on. These are the documents I consider to be authentic and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the translations will be with us in about five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, I expect a disciplined re-examination, and you must use your best efforts to avoid asking leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson. I think you should have told Mr. Nice that he should behave in a disciplined way in terms of his own examination because what we saw in respect of Mr. Jasovic could not be called that, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... anything. Were he in breach, I would have brought that to his attention and I would have disciplined him. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if misquotation and distorting statements is not in breach, statements that are not based on anything but false testimony, then you would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just now, as you were finishing your examination, you explained once again what you did. Since I wrote this down, I'm going to remind you of what you said. You said that you had the task to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. establish the number of KLA members and the quantity of weapons they had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Our operational work was geared towards the movements, activity, equipment and personnel levels of the KLA as well as the possible perpetrators of terrorist attacks because there were several such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jasovic. Within the apparatus of the Ministry of the Interior there were different people involved in different assignments. Did I understand you correctly? Your task was strictly geared towards finding out the names, the personnel levels, and identifying members of the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many statements in relation to that? How many interviews? How many friendly connections? How many interviews, as you call them, give me a very precise answer, how many of these did you conduct in order to establish the number of KLA members and the places where they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say to you that many interviews were conducted with persons of Albanian ethnicity. On these occasions, over 700 statements were taken, and several Official Notes and pieces of information, as I already said, in relation to the activities of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you involved in any other work except for seeking this information that you described as your strict assignment that you were working on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say specifically that from 1998 onwards I and my colleague Momcilo Sparavalo were strictly involved in this particular work that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of this work of yours, did you take part in any anti-terrorist action in the field using weapons? Were you involved in a search mission? Were you after perpetrators of crimes in any similar way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm saying for myself and my colleague Mr. Momcilo Sparavalo we did not take part in a single anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean, Mr. Jasovic, that all these questions that Mr. Nice put to you when he presented maps to you, various locations where bodies were allegedly found and things like that, is that all beyond the scope of your own work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to the Prosecutor that questions were put to me here. They were imposed on me, and they do not belong to my scope of work at all, and I could not answer them at all. I didn't know how to answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time you said that you felt uncomfortable. Is that what you said? Why did you use this expression that you felt uncomfortable? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I felt uncomfortable because several times I had to say I don't know, like what Bogoljub Janicevic and Danica Marinkovic said to each other or not. And then Rosja, whether he was in the building of the secretariat or not, and things like that. I mean, I really don't know. There are several questions of this kind. And of course you feel uncomfortable in that case, especially in front of this Trial Chamber, to answer that way several times, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you felt uncomfortable because you didn't know the answers to these questions, or were you uncomfortable because you were hesitant to present what you did know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have said anything I know. I felt uncomfortable because I did not know the answer to the questions put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the questions that were put to you and that you do not know the answers to, are they outside the scope of the work that are engaged in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a fact. And these are questions that would have to be put to higher supervisors, that is to say to the head of the secretariat or people closely working with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jasovic, we saw that you were a crime inspector and nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a crime inspector in 1998 and 1999 you had the exclusive assignment of finding out the names, the quantities of weapons and the localities where members of the KLA were. Did you have any other assignments?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically in 1998 and 1999, I and Mr. Sparavalo did not have any other assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jasovic, you testified here before I ever heard about you. In the Limaj case. You testified in the Limaj case. Mr. Nice informed us here that the persons whose documents appear in the Danica Marinkovic case is here at present and testifying. So you did testify in the Limaj trial?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. And I was a Prosecution witness in the trial against Isak Musliu, Limaj, and Bala.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to read part of the transcript to you from that case that has to do with questions that were put to you by Mr. Nice's side. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not in closed session? Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let us check whether it was in public session or in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some of it was in closed session. I think the majority of it was in open session. It would be for the accused to deal with this. But the parts that were dealt with in private session were largely related to registered informants or not, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, was this in open session, the parts that you intend to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Robinson. It absolutely could not have been in private session judging by the nature of the matters that were dealt with. I'm going to quote it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately I have the transcript only in English, but it will be interpreted for you so you will hear what was said. Yes. It says here -- thank you, Ms. Anoya. I wish to thank -- it says open session in parentheses. Witness Dragan Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] By Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Question: I understand, yes, thank you. Mr. Jasovic, when you took a statement or made an Official Note, did you consider it important that those documents be accurate?" [Interpretation] Your answer: "Answer: Yes." "[In English] Question: Why?" [Interpretation] Your answer: "[In English] I was not working for myself. If I wrote something that was untrue, I would be deceiving the secretariat of interior affairs, and in my view this was a great and important institution. Mr. Jasovic, did you ever force witness to give you information?"

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, Mr. Milosevic is merely quoting now some passages from the previous testimony in the Limaj case, and after quoting I expect he'll be putting a question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it coincides. I mean, it matches what you said here. Here also you said "Never." "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... such mean things." [Interpretation] That's precisely what you said then, too. Your spontaneous reaction now is the same. "[In English] Did you ever mistreat witness in order to get information?" [Interpretation] [No interpretation] "[In English] No." "Mr. Jasovic did you investigate an incident differently depending on whether or not the victim was a Serb or an Albanian or from some other ethnicity?" [Interpretation] Answer: "[In English] The Ministry of the Interior, the secretariat of the interior in Urosevac regardless of ethnic origin, religious affiliation or whatever always treated every case equally because there was division in the Ministry of the Interior."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's time for a question now. Having quoted those passages from Limaj, what is the question you're putting to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing. It says did -- the question is, rather: "[In English] You told us about the ministry of the interior but I'm interested in you personally. Did you personally investigated incidents differently depending on whether or not the victims might have been a Serb or an Albanian?" [Interpretation] And your answer: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... both Albanians, Serbs, Roma, or any other persons of any ethnic group."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you said about the way in which you worked, what you stated in response to questions put by Mr. Nice's side, does that differ in any way from what you stated here about your own conduct, about the conduct of the police, and about your work in the Secretariat of the Interior in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no difference involved whatsoever. I will always tell the truth. What I said there is what I'm saying here. You quoted my words regardless of whether it's an Albanian, a Serb or a Roma, lawful action was taken against every person if the said person acted in contravention of the law irrespective of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A large number of statements were put to you here, a large number of statements given over the past several days in 2005. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean statements ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That were taken by Mr. Nice's investigators. That were taken now in 2005.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember these statements. A few days ago, the Prosecutor presented them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you conducted your official duties in respect of which you are testifying here, that is to say when you collected statements from potential holders of information about the KLA, when did that take place, Mr. Jasovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for persons of Albanian ethnicity, I have to say this yet again, statements were taken from persons during the course of 1998, that is to say before what happened in Racak, and after what happened in Racak, and these are persons of Albanian ethnicity who wished to cooperate, voluntarily wished to cooperate with the organs of the Republic of Serbia. So these were informers, friendly contacts, and necessary information was taken from persons who were brought into custody by the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you refer to the set of documents that you compiled as interviews and that are contained in the documents of Investigating Judge Danica Marinkovic, were these documents sent to Investigating Judge Danica Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents were not sent to Danica Marinkovic for the purpose of this trial but in order to send in knowledge about the KLA staffs, the quantity of weapons they had, the possible perpetrators of attacks, et cetera in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were these statements sent to Danica Marinkovic, those statements that you took from a number -- I'm not going to say a large number or a small number, but a number of statements that you took? When was this sent to her?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly but all these statements of mine were sent to the head of the secretariat so that they could be analysed and presented systematically. I cannot remember the date. This procedure goes through the head of the crime prevention police or the head of the secretariat itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At any rate, can you recall the year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After what happened in Racak in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were all statements forwarded, then, those that were taken before and after Racak that could shed more light on Racak or only those that were taken after Racak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are statements taken before and after what happened in Racak in order to put the pieces together of everything that happened in Racak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, I have to draw your attention to this fact. All the documentation of Investigating Judge Danica Marinkovic and these that are included in the Jasovic binders testify to the proceedings that were carried out at the time when the proceedings were carried out. All the documents. And none were compiled for the purposes of these proceedings here. All the documents that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, this is commentary. It's not evidence. The accused is giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- You must avoid comments of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And may I make the point clear in case the accused has missed it, although he is trying to produce in quantities through different witnesses documents about Racak he hasn't yet produced a witness who is able to deal with them or any with investigation. That's what we've been pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milosevic, with your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Nice said is not true. Investigating Judge Danica Marinkovic was the investigating judge who was in charge of the proceedings about Racak. So for the umpteenth time Mr. Nice is not telling the truth. And also, Mr. Robinson, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to have any more of this cross-talk between the accused and the Prosecutor. Let us get on with the trial. Let us get on with the case. Let us get on with the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. In order to be able to continue examining this witness, could I get a copy of the statements that Mr. Nice showed here? Could they be placed before the witness and before me in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. There's no potential to translate everything into the Serbian language. The accused knows that perfectly well. He has been provided with more than that he would normally get in the sense that he's been provided well in advance with volumes of the materials that I would be cross-examining on, it happens to be in English, and he's able to read English and deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that this is no answer. Secondly, I don't think it's correct either, because there are a few witness statements here, and Mr. Nice claimed that they were protected witnesses, K56 or whoever. And this is probably a member of the MUP of Serbia from Urosevac. His name is protected. And not even theoretically could he have given a statement in the English language. He would have had to have given the statement in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just help there with -- in case the Chamber's not immediately familiar. Investigators in this Tribunal of course have to speak either English or French, and they deal with witnesses and potential witnesses, they therefore deal via the medium of an interpreter where necessary. The materials produced as witness statements are always produced initially in English. In certain circumstances they are translated into B/C/S but not at this stage of proceedings. They are translated into B/C/S when they're served as part of materials on an accused who is being indicted as part of the confirming materials. At this stage, cross-examination, material of this kind would never in the ordinary course of events merit translation, and there simply aren't the resources to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a rule or a practice governing this matter? Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There should be no way that he's not aware of this. Witness statements are taken in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The statements should be taken in the language of the speaker. That's the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We've done the Kosovo case, and all the Prosecution's statements were taken in English and they were later translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I understand it, the original interview was in B/C/S, and a translation of the interview would have subsequently been carried out and put into a statement form into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in what language was the original interview done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statements are -- or interviews are conducted in English via the interpreter, so it goes English question or English whatever it is, invitation to say something. The witness then replies in B/C/S. It's then translated into English, and typically the investigator who will have a laptop or notepad will write down the answer. The document -- the statement produced will then once tidied up or completed be read back through the interpreter to the witness concerned who is in a position to correct it, check it, or amend it. He then signs the document on the basis that it is indeed an English-language statement. There are one or two exceptions. One or two people, I think, have insisted on documents being made available to them there or then which of course is very time-consuming, in their own language. One in particular in this case who took that course, the leader of the KLA in Racak. I've temporarily forgotten his name. Shukri Buja made that demand. But other than that, for the entire duration of, I understand it, of this Tribunal's life and for reasons of practical good sense and necessity, statements are taken in the language of the investigators and read back via interpreter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the accused not entitled, in terms of the preparation of his case, to the statements in his language? How will he carry out his re-examination properly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When material is served as part of the confirmation material, it comes to him in the form -- in translated form. That's different. After all, the material he's getting now is material he wouldn't normally be entitled to get in any event. It's just cross-examination material that I would like to be exhibited but I'll see what happens on that application in due course. But this is not material to which he's entitled in any language other than the language it comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you agree that if this exhibit witness statements are to be exhibited you will disclose them to the accused in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, again, exhibits of course typically come in whatever language they come in which would be English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the witness statements are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness statements if they're served under 66(A)(ii), I think, are different but that's probably all. But, Your Honour, I have no objection to the material if it comes an exhibit. Of course. I'm only too anxious for it to be translated at that stage but there simply isn't time now with the huge pressure on CLSS. We would happily send everything to CLSS for translation the minute it comes our way. If we did that we'd obstruct nearly every case in this Tribunal. At the moment, for example, the translation into this accused's language and from it is being devoted to his case and his defence evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: These are not 66(A)(ii) witness statements. These are statements that you have collected for the purpose of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Your Honour, yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the position is this: You're not entitled to have these particular witness statements in your own language. They are not 66(A)(ii) witness statements. These are statements collected by the Prosecutor for the purpose of his cross-examination. If they are going to be exhibited, then there is a requirement for them to be translated. If you wish to have a particular statement looked at by the witness, then it can be placed on the ELMO and the interpreters will translate it. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you have heard that these statements were taken for the purposes of your cross-examination. Did you hear that? Have you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you happen to notice that the statements were taken for the purposes of the defence of Limaj where you are testifying as a witness for the opposite side over there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for the purposes of your cross-examination and also for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. purposes of the Limaj Defence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this, please, from your experience: In view of the fact that you have been in Kosovo for a long time, you know the KLA, you know the situation there, how far can they -- I'm not talking about Mr. Nice's investigators. I'm talking about the members of the KLA defending Limaj. How can -- how many Defence witnesses for the Limaj trial can they bring in who are going to testify whatever they're asked to testify about, whatever they're asked to testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a proper question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you heard Mr. Nice say to you that there are 50 people who claim that you beat them. Tell me, please, is it possible for the Limaj Defence or, rather, those who stand behind the Limaj Defence should collect 50 or 500 or 5.000 testimonies to say what they would like to hear them say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of April in this trial I said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't see how the witness can answer this question either. I mean, it's speculative, query relevant, all sorts of other -- probably tendentious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Don't answer the question. I agree it's tendentious, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you clarify for me which statements could Mr. Milosevic be referring to when he talks about statements taken for the Limaj Defence? Have you produced any of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, we -- well, not for the Limaj Defence. If Your Honours remember in volume 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. His point is the Limaj Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that I refer to Limaj Defence witnesses who made statements that I used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They're here, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're part of volume 2. They start -- just a few of them. Tab 19. I'm grateful to Ms. Dicklich. Your Honour may remember on looking at them -- not 19. I think it's actually -- oops. No, it's not 19. It's a little earlier than that. It's 16 I think, or 15. And Your Honour will remember that at one stage I identified tab -- no, tab 40, actually. I identified as being made for the Limaj Defence, and I think it was the accused drew to our attention, or maybe it was Your Honour, or His Honour Judge Kwon, that the title made it clear that it related to the Milosevic case and I explained that. When you go to tab 16 you'll see that the one is -- there is a statement that relates to the Defence of Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these the only two?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's the third one --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 17 as well which I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And 18. I think I referred in all to three and omitted to deal, because it wasn't necessary, with one of them and I extracted parts of what they said in each case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these were taken by the Prosecution team, were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some and some. The statements were either hand prepared in the course of -- whether it was work in the Limaj Defence or by the Defence lawyers. So that if you look, for example E at tab 14 you'd see a handwritten document that was provided to the investigator Mr. Kelly, and then if you look at 15 you'll see that Mr. Kelly reviewed it and wanting to tidy one or two things up added to it. 16 appears to be specifically prepared for the purposes of the Limaj Defence and made available to us. 17 I think is another one that was simply made available to us it certainly wasn't taken by us, otherwise it would have had a caption to that effect. And 18, again it was simply provided to us, taken in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now, Mr. Milosevic. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue, Mr. Robinson, we can see here or, rather, from the transcript as I read it out, from the Limaj trial, that Mr. Nice's side endeavoured to show the credibility of this witness, to show he was credible, whereas here Mr. Nice is trying to bring into question his credibility. So he's changed sides with this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a matter in which -- on which you can address at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When some of these statements were quoted over these past days, do you remember that it was read out to you "When I saw Jasovic testifying against Fatmir Limaj I gave the statements," et cetera, et cetera? I'm paraphrasing now, but words more or less to that effect. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the Prosecutor quoting those words to me a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have any idea about the purpose for which the statements were given which were designed to challenge your credibility date to go 1999, to impeach you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have an idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how can this witness have an idea about the purpose for which statements were given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. The witness can't help you on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you mean he can't answer when I quoted what the witness said, when he saw him testifying in the Limaj trial, fighter of the KLA, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understood you to be asking him what was the purpose for which the statements collected by the Prosecution were given and which were designed to challenge his credibility. But I don't see how the witness can assist you as to the purpose for which the Prosecutor collected the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he heard himself why the person who allegedly now is testifying to challenge his credible, because he saw him testify in the Limaj trial. That's very specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, we have heard here a number of times a question raised as to whether there was a report of any kind which was submitted with respect to the event in Racak at the topical time, material time, and by the organs in question. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. . I do remember a question like that being asked of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, since you worked in the area for a number of years, even in the Stimlje municipality to which Racak belongs for a time, if I recall correctly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from 1975 to 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, tell us, how many inhabitants does the village of Racak have, roughly speaking? I don't expect an exact figure from you, detailed statistics, but roughly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a large village has been between 250 to 300 households.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that mean, 250 to 300 households? How many inhabitants would that make it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say, but say 2.500 to 3.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. So up to 3.000 inhabitants. Would that be right? Now, if in the village of Racak there were several dozen people, can we say that the village before the event in Racak that all the inhabitants had left? Would that make it all of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the interviews that I had and all the notes and documents that I looked through, during the month of May this year I was able to see that when the terrorists, KLA terrorists, appeared in Racak and when they proceeded to arm themselves that the locals of the village knew that they would have problems, that there would be problems, that there would be clashes and conflicts between the terrorists and the police. And the local inhabitants left to go to more peaceful places. Now, in some of these statements, afterwards I happened to read that the locals of the village, that the KLA would take their food and that the KLA would seize their passenger vehicles and the machinery for repairing and building roads, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, what about the inhabitants of the village? Did they move out before these events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statements which I have, or the notes which I have, in December 1998 it says that in Racak between 10 to 15 families stayed on in Racak. However, specifically for the 15th of January, I do not have any such information, any information about that, and I really couldn't say how many households there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
